transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Aisha (Crestline Head of Security), Tom (CTO), Nora (Compliance), Evan (Platform)

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. quick intro  i'm lena, i'm the account owner, with me is marcus our se. how's that sound?
[00:08] Aisha: Thanks Lena, yep i'm aisha, head of sec at crestline. we just want to see the data controls around redaction and retention - high level, the requirements are PCI scoped fields can't be stored, audit logs for compliance, and we'd like demo of the console toggles.
[00:20] Marcus: Great, i'll demo the console and the api flags, show how redaction rules and PII detectors work, and then go into the request storage toggles  store, ephemeral, never-store  and show the logs and audit trail.
[00:30] Tom: Quick question up front, are those toggles applied at per-route level or per-organization? also curious how it works with dedicated/private deployments.
[00:38] Marcus: Good q. they can be set at multiple levels: org-wide defaults, per route, and you can override per-request with api param. for Dedicated and Private we persist audit logs the same way but you get options for on-prem storage and bring-your-own KMS.
[00:52] Nora: Are audit logs immutable? we have audits where the regulator wants chain-of-custody.
[00:57] Marcus: yes, we write append-only audit events. for private deployments you can push logs to your SIEM or S3 with object lock if you need WORM. small caveat, the hosted plan keeps an internal immutable trail for the retention window selected.
[01:12] Evan: How confident is the PII detector? we have lots of tokenized card numbers and account ids  false positives will break our downstream processing.
[01:18] Marcus: We have a tiered approach. first, simple pattern matchers for common PCI patterns (Luhn / card regex), then ML-based PII detectors that are customizable. you can add your own patterns or a scrubbing ruleset. the console shows hits and we allow soft- and hard-redaction.
[01:33] Aisha: Soft vs hard?
[01:34] Marcus: soft-redaction replaces with a token like [REDACTED_CARD] but still stores the masked placeholder so you can trace usage; hard-redaction removes the field from any persisted request and from logs  it's never written. hard-redaction is required for PCI scoped data.
[01:49] Aisha: does hard-redaction interfere with debugability?
[01:51] Marcus: it does reduce observability. that's why we support fine-grained rules: for QA routes you might use soft, for production payment routes you set hard and then have tracing via non-PII ids only. also you can enable sampling for redacted logs if you need raw traces under strict controls.
[02:05] [00:02:05] Lena: i'll pause the demo and share my screen  console home. bear with me - mm, permissions popped, great.
[02:14] [00:02:14] Marcus: you should see the project settings, under data controls -> retention & redaction. here's the org default: 30 days for requests, 90 days for metrics; you can change it. you can also toggle default request_storage to 'store' / 'ephemeral' / 'never_store'.
[02:32] Tom: if we choose never_store at org-level can devs still override?
[02:35] Marcus: no, never_store at org-level is a policy that cannot be overridden by lower levels unless you have an admin exception. policy enforcement is RBAC'd.
[02:45] Nora: what about partial retention? say we want to retain non-PII text but strip PII and keep the remaining content for 180 days.
[02:52] Marcus: yeah you can apply transformation rules  redact PII fields, then persist the transformed text. the retention window applies to the stored artifact post-transformation. we'll show an example in the api demo.
[03:00] [00:03:00] Marcus: switching to an API example. here's curl to call generation with header "x-redwood-request-storage: never_store" and a "redaction-rules" json blob. i'll paste the payload.
[03:12] Marcus (typing): curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H "x-redwood-request-storage: never_store" -d '{"prompt":"process payment 4111-1111-1111-1111 amount $100" , "redaction_rules": [{"pattern":"card","type":"pci"}] }'
[03:35] Evan: so that header overrides route default, and never_store guarantees nothing persists?
[03:39] Marcus: correct for hosted - the request body and the model output are not written to persistent storage. ephemeral logs still exist in memory for the duration of the request for routing/tracing, but not to disk. for private deployments you can enforce never_store at network level.
[03:53] Aisha: ok, about KV cache  will card fragments ever be written to cache?
[03:57] Marcus: we treat KV cache separately. we scrub the cache with the same rules. if something matches hard-redaction it won't be cached. caching behavior is configurable per model profile.
[04:08] [00:04:08] Tom: are the redaction rules synchronous? could there be a race where we log before the rule runs?
[04:13] Marcus: rules run at ingestion stage before any persistence; telemetry events for routing are emitted but don't include request body unless allowed. there was a note about early-path logging in older runtimes but current releases fix that, but i'll note the version for you.
[04:26] Lena: small aside  regulators often ask for proof of deletion, do you provide deletion proofs?
[04:30] Marcus: yes we provide deletion receipt events and a deletion audit record. in private you can retain logs locally and validate deletion using object storage checksums and our audit export.
[04:40] Nora: what about key management? we need BYOK and HSM for production.
[04:44] Marcus: supported. you can plug in your KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure KeyVault) or our HSM integrations for Private. encrypted at rest and in transit, with access logs forwarded to your SIEM.
[04:57] Aisha: any customer examples for payments?
[05:00] Lena: we have a few banks and payments customers, e.g., MeridianPay, Harbor payments, we ran a pilot with redaction rules and dedicated capacity. happy to introduce references if you want.
[05:10] Aisha: yes please, references matter.
[05:12] [00:05:12] Marcus: back to the console: here's the redaction ruleset editor. it's a list of rules  regex, ML-detect, post-processing transforms. you can test a sample payload in the UI. i'll paste a test with a card number  note the detector flags it and you can preview the soft and hard outputs.
[05:30] [00:05:30] Marcus: demo clip: input = "charge 4242 4242 4242 4242 for $25 to user john" -> soft-redaction preview: "charge [REDACTED_CARD] for $25 to user john" -> hard-redaction preview: "charge for $25 to user john"
[05:48] Nora: nice  can we get an export of those test results? we need them for audit.
[05:51] Marcus: yes, you can export to csv or push to S3. export includes rule hit metadata, timestamps, and the sanitized artifact.
[05:58] Evan: how about retention for embeddings and vector indexes? we are using embeddings for search over support transcripts.
[06:05] Marcus: embeddings are considered derived artifacts; you can control retention separately. we also support PII scrubbing prior to embedding generation; if you mark text as never_store, you can still create ephemeral embeddings for immediate use but not persist them.
[06:20] Tom: curious about cost tradeoffs  never_store reduces data footprint but increases CPU for redaction and for on-the-fly transforms, is there guidance?
[06:28] Marcus: yes, we surface estimated cost impact in the console Optimize tab. we show token cost delta for redaction, additional CPU for ML detectors, and recommendations like using regex-first strategy to reduce ML invocations.
[06:40] [00:06:40] Lena: i'm going to open the Optimize tab  this is where the platform suggests batching/caching and quantization to save costs, but for data controls it gives you estimated latency and cost for redaction rules.
[06:53] Marcus: the Optimize suggestions can create profiles  e.g., 'payments-prod' with hard-redaction + never_store + dedicated model with low-latency profile. you can then apply the profile to routes.
[07:06] Aisha: for PCI, regulators often want SSO and RBAC. can we lock down who can change redaction rules?
[07:13] Marcus: yes RBAC controls are granular. we have an admin role, security operator role, and you can restrict rule editing and policy changes. changes are audited.
[07:22] Nora: do we get alerts on policy drift? if someone changes retention or flips never_store to store?
[07:27] Marcus: we have config-change alerts and drift detection. you can wire it to pager duty or slack; changes require approval for protected routes.
[07:36] [00:07:36] Lena: i'm going to show the audit logs view. here's a sample event stream  we show event type, actor, change diff and a request_id. sensitive content never appears in the event body, just metadata.
[07:50] Evan: can we stream those events to our SIEM in realtime?
[07:53] Marcus: yes, via webhook or direct forwarder. for private deployments you can keep the forwarder local. we support JSON lines and syslog formats.
[08:02] Tom: about benchmarks  we'd like to run sample payment flows with our compliance dataset. what's typical throughput and latency impact when redaction is enabled?
[08:11] Marcus: depends on rules complexity. simple regex adds negligible latency (<5ms), ML-based PII detection could add 30-80ms per request depending on model profile. batching and caching reduce overall token cost; Optimize will simulate throughput. we'll do a pilot to measure with your payloads.
[08:26] Aisha: for the pilot, can we get an NDA or data handling agreement before we share sample payloads?
[08:31] Lena: yes, we'll attach our DPA and we can execute an NDA. i'll include legal touchpoints.
[08:36] [00:08:36] Marcus: quick note on edge cases  some customers have encrypted fields in payloads. we support pre-ingest transform hooks so you can decrypt locally and re-encrypt ephemeral, but that requires private deployment or a secure tunnel.
[08:50] Nora: we also need retention to line up with our e-discovery process; can you retain search indexes longer than raw requests?
[08:56] Marcus: yes you can set separate retention policies for derived artifacts like embeddings, indexes, and metrics. you can also pin certain artifacts for longer retention if regulator requires.
[09:07] Lena: we're ~10 minutes left, want to run through next steps.
[09:11] Aisha: yes please.
[09:13] Lena: we'll send SOC2, security whitepaper, and references. Marcus will own the benchmark plan; Evan will share a sanitized sample dataset or request an NDA. we'll schedule a 1-hour benchmark sesh next week.
[09:25] Evan: i'll talk to legal and share what fields we can provide.
[09:28] Nora: one more: can you include a sample deletion receipt for regulator review?
[09:32] Marcus: yes i'll include an example deletion receipt export.
[09:35] Tom: thanks, this was helpful. two small asks: include pricing for dedicated committed capacity, and an architecture note for private on-prem deployment.
[09:44] Lena: will do.
[09:46] [00:09:46] Marcus: final quick FAQ bits  function/tool calls: we redact function inputs too; streaming: streaming tokens can be masked on the fly; logging: token-level logs are optional.
[09:59] Aisha: any blockers we should expect?
[10:01] Marcus: only time to run the pilot and finalize NDA. technical blockers rare, mainly around integrating BYOK or SIEM endpoints.
[10:09] Lena: all right thanks everyone. i'll send notes and next steps after the call.
[10:13] Aisha: thanks, bye.
